title: Uranus' Moon Ariel May Have Had a 100-Mile-Deep Ocean
summary: Scientists have found new evidence that Ariel, one of Uranus' moons, may have once contained a vast ocean beneath its icy surface. The research, published in the journal Icarus, suggests that ocean could have been more than 100 miles (170 kilometers) deep. For comparison, the Pacific Ocean averages only about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) deep. "Ariel is pretty unique in terms of icy moons," said Alex Patthoff, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute and co-author of the paper. Ariel is the brightest of Uranus' moons and the second closest to the planet. It's only 720 miles (1,159 kilometers) across — about the distance from Tucson to Salt Lake City — making it the fourth-largest moon in the Uranian system. Despite its small size, Ariel has a surprisingly complex surface. Ancient impact craters sit next to much younger terrain. Some smooth areas may have formed through cryovolcanism — a process where water, ice, or other volatile materials erupt from an icy world instead of molten rock. The moon is also covered in fractures, ridges, and grabens (areas where sections of the crust have dropped down). Some of these structures are larger than almost anywhere else in the Solar System. To understand what created these features, researchers modeled Ariel's past interior and orbit. They focused on orbital eccentricity — how much an orbit differs from a perfect circle. As a moon travels around its planet, gravitational forces stretch and squeeze it, creating tidal stress. "First, we mapped out the larger structures that we see on the surface, then we used a computer program to model the tidal stresses," Patthoff said. "By combining the model with what we see on the surface, we can make inferences about Ariel's past eccentricity and how thick the ocean might have been." The team found Ariel's orbit may once have had an eccentricity of about 0.04 — roughly 40 times greater than today. That's still nearly circular, but it would have greatly amplified tidal forces. For comparison, it's about four times more eccentric than Jupiter's moon Europa, whose icy shell is heavily fractured by similar forces. "In order to create those fractures, you have to have either a really thin ice on a really big ocean, or a higher eccentricity and a smaller ocean," Patthoff said. "But either way, we need an ocean to be able to create the fractures that we are seeing on Ariel's surface." This is the second study in a series. Last year, the same team reported similar findings for Miranda, another icy moon of Uranus. Together, the results suggest more than one moon in the Uranian system may have had a subsurface ocean. "We are finding evidence that the Uranus system may harbor twin ocean worlds," said co-author Tom Nordheim of Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. "Unfortunately, we've only seen the southern hemispheres of Ariel and Miranda. But our results can give us predictions of what a future spacecraft might see on the moons' unimaged northern hemispheres." Scientists still don't know exactly when Ariel's ocean existed or how long it lasted. But the findings provide a foundation for future studies on how subsurface oceans on distant icy worlds form, evolve, and possibly disappear.
why_it_matters: The study shows how much of our own Solar System is still unexplored: two small moons of a planet visited only once may have hidden oceans, and liquid water is the first thing scientists look for when asking whether life could exist beyond Earth. It also gives mission planners a set of testable predictions for the next spacecraft sent to Uranus.

background_read: Uranus (the seventh planet from the Sun, a huge ball of ice and gas that orbits tipped over on its side) has a crowd of known moons, but scientists have only ever had one close-up look at the whole system. NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft (an uncrewed probe launched in the 1970s that toured the outer planets) flew past Uranus in the 1980s and photographed only the southern halves of its moons, which is why researchers today still combine those old images with computer models.

Moons with hidden oceans are not rare in the outer Solar System. Jupiter's moon Europa (a world whose cracked icy shell is the classic example) and Saturn's moon Enceladus both show strong signs of liquid water beneath the ice. The heat that keeps such water from freezing usually comes from tidal stress — the same gravitational squeezing that the new Ariel study modelled.

Icarus is a peer-reviewed journal where planetary scientists publish this kind of modelling work, and the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (a research lab that helps build spacecraft and study the outer Solar System) took part in the analysis. A future spacecraft mission to Uranus has been ranked a top priority by planetary scientists, because almost everything known about its moons comes from a single brief flyby decades ago.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — planetary scientists and mission planners
perspectives.description: The paper adds a second possible ocean world in the Uranian system, turning an oddity into a pattern. That strengthens the case for sending a dedicated Uranus orbiter, since computer models can now predict where a spacecraft should look.

The ocean is inferred, not seen: no instrument has ever sampled Ariel's interior, and only its southern hemisphere has been photographed. The team also cannot say when the ocean existed or how long it survived, so the claim rests on matching surface fractures to an orbital model.

Ariel fits a growing family of 'ocean worlds' — Europa, Enceladus, Titan and now possibly Miranda and Ariel — where tidal heating keeps water liquid far from the Sun. That suggests hidden oceans may be common rather than exceptional on icy moons.

The results are framed as predictions for a future Uranus mission, which could image the moons' unmapped northern hemispheres and test the tidal-stress models directly. Until then, each new modelling study adds a piece rather than closing the question.
